title: Haloalkanes from Alcohols: HX, PCl₃, PCl₅ and SOCl₂
summary: One rule: R–OH → R–X, the OH group is replaced by a halogen; only the reagent and its by-products change. HX gives water (anhydrous ZnCl₂ for 1° and 2° alcohols; reactivity 3° > 2° > 1°), PCl₃ gives H₃PO₃ (1 PCl₃ : 3 R–OH), PCl₅ gives POCl₃ + HCl, and SOCl₂ gives SO₂ + HCl, two gases that escape, so the alkyl chloride is pure. Phenol does not react this way: its C–O bond has partial double-bond character.

notes.title: 07 – Haloalkanes from Alcohols
notes.blurb: all four reagents with equations, by-products, conditions and solved examples

keyPoints: **Rule:** R–OH → R–X. The OH group leaves and a halogen takes its place.
**HX:** R–OH + HCl → R–Cl + H₂O; anhydrous **ZnCl₂** for 1° and 2°; 3° just shaken with conc. HCl. Reactivity **3° > 2° > 1°**.
R–Br: NaBr + H₂SO₄ (HBr); R–I: heat with NaI or KI in 95% H₃PO₄.
**PCl₃:** 3 R–OH + PCl₃ → 3 R–Cl + **H₃PO₃**. PBr₃ and PI₃ are made **in situ** from red P + Br₂ / I₂.
**SOCl₂:** R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + **SO₂↑ + HCl↑**: both gases escape, so the product is pure. The best reagent.
**Not for phenol:** its C–O bond has partial double-bond character, so aryl halides cannot be made this way.

blocks.p: In every method the **OH group of the alcohol is replaced by a halogen**. What changes from reagent to reagent is the **by-products**, and that decides how pure the alkyl halide is.

list: 1° and 2° alcohols need **anhydrous ZnCl₂**; dry HCl gas is passed through the alcohol, or the alcohol is heated in conc. aqueous HCl.
3° alcohols react on simply **shaking with conc. HCl at room temperature**.
Order of reactivity with a given HX: **3° > 2° > 1°**.
Alkyl bromide: constant-boiling HBr (48%), or NaBr + H₂SO₄. Alkyl iodide: heat with NaI or KI in 95% H₃PO₄.

blocks.p: One PCl₃ reacts with **three** alcohol molecules. **PBr₃ and PI₃** are generated **in situ** from red phosphorus and bromine or iodine.
Both by-products are **gases that escape**, so the alkyl chloride is left **pure**. That is why SOCl₂ is preferred.

blocks.p: Phenol does **not** give chlorobenzene with HCl, PCl₃, PCl₅ or SOCl₂. In phenol the C–O bond has **partial double-bond character** (resonance with the ring), so it is stronger than a single bond and is not broken. These methods do not make aryl halides.
